title: Which runtime starts
cards/0/body:
The build writes app.runtimeconfig.json from the project TargetFramework. The key data in it is the framework name and version. This is the minimum version, not the one you built against: for net8.0 it says 8.0.0.

configProperties receives runtime settings from the project: GC mode, invariant globalization and others. The runtime reads them at startup, and code sees them through AppContext. You can edit them right in the file on the server, without rebuilding.
cards/0/deep: A web app has a frameworks array instead of framework, for example Microsoft.AspNetCore.App; NETCore.App comes in through the runtimeconfig of ASP.NET Core itself. The RuntimeFrameworkVersion project property raises the minimum version for a framework-dependent app, and for a self-contained one it sets the exact version that ships with it.
cards/1/body:
How to pick an installed version when 8.0.0 is requested is decided by the rollForward policy. The patch version is almost always the latest: that is how an app gets security fixes without a rebuild.

  • Minor (the default): the same major and minor, latest patch. If that minor is missing, the nearest higher minor. It never moves to another major version.
  • Major: like Minor, but if the requested major is missing entirely, it takes the nearest higher major, at its lowest minor.
  • LatestPatch: latest patch only, minor roll-forward is disabled.
  • LatestMinor: the highest minor of the same major, even if the requested one is present.
  • LatestMajor: the highest version of all, even if the requested one is present.
  • Disable: exactly the specified version, no patches. For testing only.
cards/1/deep:
Since .NET 5 there have been no minor releases: every version is X.0.patch. So in practice Minor means "latest patch of your own major", and the real choice is between Minor, Major and LatestMajor.

Prerelease versions (preview, rc) are not picked by default when a release version is requested. The DOTNET_ROLL_FORWARD_TO_PRERELEASE=1 variable changes that.
cards/2/q: An app targets net8.0 and rollForward is not set. The machine has only runtimes 9.0.6 and 10.0.0 installed. What happens?
cards/2/options/0: It does not start: "You must install or update .NET"
cards/2/options/3: It runs on 9.0.6 with a console warning
cards/2/explain: The default is Minor, and it never moves to another major version. To run on 9, set rollForward to Major: in the project, with the DOTNET_ROLL_FORWARD variable or with the --roll-forward option.
cards/2/wrong/1: That is what the Major policy would do. Minor, the default, does not move to another major version.
cards/2/wrong/2: LatestMajor would pick the newest one.
cards/3/q: Match each policy with its behavior
cards/3/pairs/0/1: Next major, only if its own is missing
cards/3/pairs/1/1: Newest installed, even if its own is present
cards/4/q: An app requests 8.0.0 with rollForward = Major. Installed: 8.2.3, 8.4.5, 9.0.6 and 9.7.8 (an example with minor versions, so the rule is visible). What does hostfxr pick?
cards/4/explain: Major version 8 is present, so Major behaves like Minor: 8.0 is missing, so the nearest higher minor, 8.2, at its latest patch, 8.2.3. This example comes from the Microsoft documentation.
cards/4/wrong/1: Major moves to the next major only when its own major is missing entirely. And 8.x is installed.
cards/4/wrong/2: LatestMajor would take the newest one.
cards/4/wrong/3: LatestMinor would take the highest minor. Minor and Major take the nearest one.
cards/5/title: Where to set it and who wins
cards/5/body:
The policy can be set in four places. The <RollForward> project property is simply written into runtimeconfig.json. At startup the order is as follows, each one overriding the previous:

  • rollForward in runtimeconfig.json;
  • the DOTNET_ROLL_FORWARD environment variable;
  • the --roll-forward option at launch.

The "version 2" scenario: you shipped a tool for .NET 8 with Major so it runs where only .NET 10 is installed. Convenient, but the app will run on a runtime you never tested it on. Microsoft publishes behavior changes between major versions as breaking changes.
cards/6/q: A net8.0 app should run on .NET 8 when it is present, and otherwise on the nearest newer major version. Complete the project.
cards/6/explain: Major sticks to its own major version while it is present and moves to the next one only when it is missing. LatestMajor would go to the newest one even with .NET 8 installed.
cards/7/title: Self-contained: the runtime travels with the app
cards/7/body:
A framework-dependent app is small and uses the machine-wide .NET. When an admin installs a patch, the app gets it on its next start.

A self-contained app carries the runtime with it: hostfxr, hostpolicy, coreclr and the libraries sit in the app folder. It is published for a specific platform (a RID such as linux-x64) and weighs tens of megabytes.

The price: the runtime version is chosen at publish time, the latest patch the SDK knows about. There is no roll-forward. When a security fix comes out, you must rebuild and redeploy the app.
cards/8/q: What is true for a self-contained app? Select all.
cards/8/options/1: Security patches arrive when a new .NET is installed on the machine
cards/8/options/2: It is published for a specific RID
cards/8/options/3: The rollForward policy has no effect on runtime choice
cards/8/options/4: The same output runs on both Windows and Linux
cards/8/explain: The runtime sits in the app folder, and a global install is neither needed nor used. Hence the downside: the runtime can be updated only by a new publish. The native parts of the runtime differ per OS, so publishing targets a RID.
cards/9/body:
PublishSingleFile=true appends a bundle to the apphost: the managed assemblies, runtimeconfig.json and deps.json. It works for both self-contained and framework-dependent apps.

At startup the managed assemblies are not extracted to disk: the runtime reads them straight from the bundle, in memory. Native libraries may stay as separate files next to it. The IncludeNativeLibrariesForSelfExtract property puts them inside too, but then they are extracted to a temp folder at startup.

The consequence for code: an assembly no longer has a path on disk. Assembly.Location returns an empty string, and Assembly.CodeBase throws. For files next to the program use AppContext.BaseDirectory.
cards/9/deep: The extraction folder is set by DOTNET_BUNDLE_EXTRACT_BASE_DIR; without it, it is $HOME/.net on Linux and macOS and %TEMP%\.net on Windows. Under systemd $HOME may be unset, so set the variable explicitly. The single-file analyzer flags risky calls with IL3000 and related codes. Environment.ProcessPath (since .NET 6) gives the path to the exe itself.
cards/10/q: The app is published with PublishSingleFile=true. Which line does not give the path you need?
cards/10/explain: The assembly was loaded from the bundle, it has no file, and Location is an empty string. ProcessPath and BaseDirectory work: the first points at the exe itself, the second at its folder.
cards/11/title: Trimming: what is removed cannot be loaded
cards/11/body:
PublishTrimmed=true turns on ILLink: it walks static references from the entry point and removes from the app and the framework libraries everything it did not reach. It works only for self-contained apps: the machine-wide shared runtime cannot be trimmed.

What breaks is anything the code finds at run time: reflection by string names, Assembly.LoadFrom with plugins, Reflection.Emit. The analyzer flags such places with IL2xxx warnings, and the [RequiresUnreferencedCode] and [DynamicallyAccessedMembers] attributes help it understand the code.

For loading this means: a separately built plugin may call a framework method that was removed, and get a MissingMethodException.
cards/11/deep:
TrimMode sets the scope: full trims all assemblies, partial only those marked IsTrimmable. Feature switches such as EventSourceSupport=false or InvariantGlobalization=true do two things: they let ILLink remove code, and they write the value into runtimeconfig.json so the runtime does not take the removed path.

Trimming turns off incompatible features: built-in COM interop and DOTNET_STARTUP_HOOKS startup hooks. The SDK does not support trimming for WPF and WinForms. Native AOT always trims; the lesson on ahead-of-time compilation in the first unit covers it.
cards/12/q: A plugin host is published with PublishTrimmed=true. Plugins are compiled separately and loaded from a folder. What is the risk?
cards/12/options/0: A plugin may call a framework API that is gone after trimming
cards/12/options/1: None: ILLink sees the plugins folder at publish time
cards/12/options/2: Plugins will not load: a trimmed app has no AssemblyLoadContext
cards/12/options/3: Plugins get trimmed on first load
cards/12/explain: ILLink kept only what the host itself needs. It never saw the plugin, so methods needed only by the plugin may have been removed. This is a known incompatibility: plugin systems and trimming do not get along.
cards/12/wrong/2: Assembly loading works; the analyzer just warns about it. The problem is missing code inside the framework.
cards/12/wrong/3: Trimming happens once, at publish time. Nothing is trimmed at run time.
